messages.author: 23b384a0d94b9b78
messages.subject: framing secr models
parts:
Hi, 
I am new to SECR and have been looking at the secr vignettes and some papers to understand how secr models are framed. I have one question (it is very basic). I have seen that sometimes people have specified only one of the parameters (g0 or lambda). So does that mean the other parameter is constant (g0~1) for that model?

Thank you,

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: framing secr models
parts: I understand your confusion. g0 and lambda0 are intercept parameters corresponding to alternative ways of specifying the detection function, so you use one or the other. g0 is the appropriate parameter when the detection function is specified in terms of probability of detection vs distance (detectfn = 'HN', 'EX' etc.). lambda0 is the appropriate parameter when the detection function is expressed in terms of the hazard of detection vs distance (detectfn = 'HHN', 'HEX' etc.). The default detectfn is 'HN', so by default g0 is used. A detection function specified in terms of the hazard of detection has some properties that make manipulation easier (e.g. computing expected counts in secrdesign), and my intuition suggests it is closer to the corresponding home range model (e.g., circular bivariate normal = 'HHN'). But in practice no-one really minds which you use. Check ?detectfn.

messages.subject: Re: framing secr models
parts: Thank you for the clear explanation Murray. One follow up question. I have also seen some people not specifying the sigma parameter. As far as I understand, sigma is the declining slope of the curve (the scale parameter?). What does the lack of sigma mean? Sorry I am not from a statistics background so I am trying to understand the basics as far as possible.

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: framing secr models
parts: sigma appears in every model; if it's not mentioned then it will be assumed constant (sigma ~1). This goes for any model parameter. (An extra point - exactly what is meant by 'sigma' also depends on the choice of detectfn, so don't compare between models with different detectfn).
